On one end, you may have the parents who shut a person out and are abusive, and on the opposite side you may have parents that are totally okay with it and throw you a "Coming Out" party. Most parents are going to fall somewhere in the middle. It is important to remember that their feelings may change over time. Many parents struggle at first, but they love their kids and get better with it over time. If you decide to tell them, consider taking someone along to support you. Plan ahead on what you want to say. It can be an emotional time, so do what you need to do to take care of yourself. If you need to, leave. You don't have to stay anywhere where someone is being cruel to you. I wish you well, and good luck. Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

It sounds like you're navigating a really challenging situation, and I want you to know that your feelings are valid. Coming to terms with your identity can be difficult, especially when you feel unable to share that part of yourself with your family. 

One supportive step you can take is to seek out a trusted professional, like a therapist or a life coach. They can provide you with a safe space to explore your feelings and help you develop strategies for coping. If you're not ready to share your identity with your family yet, consider telling them that you want to talk to someone for general support, such as help with school or other stresses.

Building a community of support outside of your family can also be incredibly helpful. Look for local LGBTQ+ support groups or online communities where you can connect with others who may have similar experiences. Speaking to someone who understands can make you feel less isolated.

In the meantime, give yourself permission to explore your identity in a way that feels safe and comfortable for you. This could involve journaling about your feelings, reading literature that resonates with your experience, or simply taking time to reflect on what being your true self means to you.

Remember, you are not alone in this journey, and there are people who will accept and support you for who you are. Take your time, and prioritize your safety and well-being as you navigate these feelings. If things ever feel overwhelming, don't hesitate to reach out for immediate help from a mental health professional. You deserve to feel supported and understood.
